questions.stem: How is fission usually induced in a uranium-235 nucleus in a reactor?
options: The nucleus spontaneously emits a beta particle and becomes plutonium
The nucleus captures a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei and several neutrons
The nucleus captures a fast proton and splits into two equal halves, releasing no neutrons
The nucleus is struck by a gamma ray and emits an alpha particle
questions.explanation: Capturing a neutron makes the nucleus unstable, and it splits into two medium-sized fission fragments, releasing two or three fast neutrons and a large amount of energy. Neutrons are used because, being uncharged, they are not repelled by the nucleus.

questions.stem: Why do the neutrons released in fission make a chain reaction possible?
options: They are positively charged, so they are attracted to other uranium nuclei
They join together to form new uranium-235 nuclei that then split
On average more than one is released, and each can induce another fission
Each one carries enough energy to split several nuclei at once by itself
questions.explanation: Each fission releases on average more than one neutron. If at least one of these goes on to cause another fission, the process sustains itself, which is a chain reaction.

questions.stem: A reactor runs steadily at constant power. On average, how many neutrons from each fission go on to cause another fission?
options: More than one
Fewer than one
None at all
Exactly one
questions.explanation: At steady power, each fission leads on average to exactly one more fission, so the rate of fission stays constant; the reactor is said to be critical. More than one would make the power grow, and fewer than one would make it die away.

questions.stem: How is a reactor started up from shutdown?
options: Control rods are withdrawn until each fission causes slightly more than one further fission
Control rods are pushed fully in until the fission rate increases from zero
The moderator is drained so that neutrons travel faster and cause many more fissions each
Coolant flow is stopped so that the core heats up and fissions begin
questions.explanation: Withdrawing control rods means fewer neutrons are absorbed, so the average number of fissions caused by each fission rises above one and the power grows. When it reaches the desired level the rods are adjusted so that the ratio is exactly one.

questions.stem: In an emergency, a reactor is shut down within seconds. What happens to the chain reaction?
options: The fuel rods are cooled until the uranium nuclei can no longer split
Control rods drop in and absorb neutrons, so each fission causes fewer than one more
Control rods are pulled out and release stored neutrons, so the fissions stop at once
The moderator is heated until it absorbs every neutron produced in the core
questions.explanation: Inserting the control rods fully absorbs so many neutrons that, on average, each fission causes fewer than one further fission, and the chain reaction dies away. Cooling the fuel does not stop fission.

questions.stem: What happens to most of the neutrons released by fission in a reactor core?
options: They are reflected back into the fuel by the control rods
Many are absorbed by other nuclei or escape without causing fission
All of them go on to cause further fissions in uranium-235
They decay into protons and electrons before they leave the fuel rod
questions.explanation: Neutrons can be captured by uranium-238, the moderator, the control rods or the structure, or escape from the core altogether. Only some cause further fissions, which is why the design must ensure that on average exactly one does.

questions.stem: Why must the neutrons released by fission be slowed down to keep a chain reaction going in uranium-235?
options: Fast neutrons decay into protons before they can reach another nucleus
Uranium-235 is far more likely to undergo fission when it captures a slow neutron
Fast neutrons are positively charged, so they are strongly repelled by uranium-235 nuclei
Slow neutrons carry more kinetic energy, so they split the nucleus more easily
questions.explanation: The neutrons from fission are very fast, and uranium-235 rarely captures them. Slowed to low speeds, they are much more likely to be captured and cause fission. Slow neutrons have less kinetic energy, not more.

questions.stem: What is the job of the moderator in a fission reactor?
options: To absorb neutrons and control the reaction rate
To carry thermal energy away to the turbines
To stop radiation escaping from the building
To slow down fast neutrons through collisions
questions.explanation: The moderator slows the fast neutrons from fission by repeated collisions until they are slow enough to cause fission in uranium-235. Absorbing neutrons is the job of the control rods.

questions.stem: Why are materials with light nuclei, such as the hydrogen in water, good moderators?
options: Light nuclei absorb neutrons completely, removing their energy in one step
Light nuclei are positively charged and repel the neutrons, slowing them down
A neutron loses most of its kinetic energy when it collides with a much heavier nucleus
A neutron loses most kinetic energy when it collides with a nucleus of similar mass
questions.explanation: In an elastic collision, a neutron hitting a nucleus of about its own mass can transfer most or all of its kinetic energy, as one billiard ball hitting another. Bouncing off a heavy nucleus, it rebounds with nearly the same speed. Neutrons are uncharged, so there is no electrostatic repulsion.

questions.stem: Natural uranium is about 0.7% uranium-235. What does enrichment do?
options: Increases the proportion of uranium-238 in the uranium
Converts uranium-238 into uranium-235 by adding a neutron
Removes all radioactive isotopes from the uranium fuel
Increases the proportion of uranium-235 in the uranium
questions.explanation: Enrichment separates the isotopes so that the fuel contains a higher fraction of fissile uranium-235, around a few per cent for power reactors. It cannot change one isotope into another.

questions.stem: Why does a chain reaction not proceed in natural uranium in a water-moderated reactor, but can in enriched fuel?
options: Uranium-238 releases far too many neutrons, which make the chain reaction run out of control
Uranium-235 cannot undergo fission unless uranium-238 is completely removed first
Natural uranium is too dense for neutrons to move between its nuclei at all
Too many neutrons are absorbed by uranium-238 for enough to reach the scarce uranium-235
questions.explanation: In natural uranium, more than 99% of the nuclei are uranium-238, which mostly absorbs neutrons without fissioning. Raising the uranium-235 fraction makes it likely enough that a neutron causes another fission, so on average one fission can lead to another.

questions.stem: Uranium is enriched by spinning uranium hexafluoride gas in centrifuges. What property allows the isotopes to be separated?
options: The difference in chemical reactivity between uranium-235 and uranium-238
The difference in electric charge between the two isotopes' nuclei
The difference in the number of electrons in the two isotopes' atoms
The small difference in mass between uranium-235 and uranium-238
questions.explanation: Isotopes of an element are chemically identical and have the same nuclear charge and number of electrons, so they cannot be separated chemically. Molecules containing uranium-238 are slightly heavier and move towards the outside of a spinning centrifuge, which allows a gradual separation.

questions.stem: What is the function of the control rods in a fission reactor?
options: To carry energy from the core to the steam generator
To absorb neutrons and so control the rate of fission
To slow fast neutrons down so that they cause fission
To hold the enriched uranium fuel inside the core
questions.explanation: Control rods contain neutron-absorbing materials such as boron or cadmium. Moving them in absorbs more neutrons and slows the chain reaction; moving them out speeds it up.

questions.stem: What is the main job of the coolant in a water-moderated power reactor?
options: To shield workers from gamma rays outside the building
To enrich the fuel as it flows past the fuel rods
To carry thermal energy from the core to produce steam
To absorb neutrons so the chain reaction stays steady
questions.explanation: The coolant, water in this type of reactor, flows through the core, absorbs the energy released by fission and carries it to a heat exchanger or straight to a turbine, where steam drives the generator. Absorbing neutrons is the job of the control rods.

questions.stem: In a water-moderated reactor, the same water acts as both moderator and coolant. What two jobs does it do?
options: It absorbs neutrons by capture and shields the turbines from gamma rays
It speeds up neutrons and carries thermal energy into the fuel rods
It absorbs neutrons by capture and condenses the steam that leaves the turbine
It slows neutrons by collisions and carries thermal energy out of the core
questions.explanation: The hydrogen nuclei in water are effective at slowing neutrons, so water moderates. Flowing through the core, the same water also removes the energy released by fission.

questions.stem: What do the fuel rods of a water-moderated power reactor contain?
options: Pellets of enriched uranium, usually as uranium oxide
Boron or cadmium to absorb excess neutrons
Graphite blocks to slow the fast neutrons down
Pure uranium-238 with all of the uranium-235 removed
questions.explanation: Fuel rods are sealed metal tubes filled with pellets of enriched uranium oxide, where the fission takes place. Boron and cadmium belong in control rods, and graphite is a moderator in some other reactor designs.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the thick steel and concrete containment structure around a reactor?
options: To store the steam before it is sent to drive the turbines
To stop radioactive material and radiation escaping to the environment
To slow down neutrons so they can cause further fissions in the fuel
To absorb neutrons and keep the chain reaction running steadily
questions.explanation: The containment and shielding absorb radiation from the core and are designed to hold in radioactive material even if there is an accident inside. Slowing neutrons is the moderator's job.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes how a fission power station produces electricity?
options: Fission produces light, which falls on solar cells around the core
Fission heats coolant, which makes steam that turns a turbine and generator
Fission produces electrons directly, which flow out of the core as electric current
Fission heats the control rods, which turn the generator as they expand
questions.explanation: The kinetic energy of the fission fragments becomes thermal energy in the fuel. The coolant carries it away to make steam, which drives a turbine connected to a generator, just as in a coal-fired station.

questions.stem: In what form does most of the energy released in a fission event first appear?
options: Potential energy of the neutrons left behind
Kinetic energy of the two fission fragments
Chemical energy stored in the new molecules
Electrical energy in the reactor's cables
questions.explanation: Most of the energy released appears as kinetic energy of the two positively charged fragments, which fly apart and then collide with surrounding atoms, heating the fuel. Smaller amounts are carried by the neutrons and gamma rays.

questions.stem: In one fission event, the reactants (uranium-235 and a neutron) have a total mass of 3.91965 × 10⁻²⁵ kg and the products have a total mass of 3.91656 × 10⁻²⁵ kg. How much energy is released? Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Δm = 3.91965 × 10⁻²⁵ − 3.91656 × 10⁻²⁵ = 3.09 × 10⁻²⁸ kg, and E = Δmc² = 3.09 × 10⁻²⁸ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 2.78 × 10⁻¹¹ J. Multiplying by c instead of c² gives 9.27 × 10⁻²⁰ J.

questions.stem: A reactor core releases thermal energy at 3.0 × 10⁹ W. Each fission releases about 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J. About how many fissions occur each second?
questions.explanation: Power is energy per second, so the number of fissions per second is 3.0 × 10⁹/(3.2 × 10⁻¹¹) ≈ 9.4 × 10¹⁹. Multiplying instead gives 9.6 × 10⁻², which is far too few to produce gigawatts.

questions.stem: Why is the total mass of the products of a fission reaction less than the total mass of the reactants?
options: The missing mass has been converted into the energy released, E = Δmc²
Some of the mass escapes as neutrons, which are too small to be counted
Mass is destroyed in nuclear reactions, and no energy is involved
The products are cooler than the reactants, so their particles weigh less
questions.explanation: The energy released in fission comes from a decrease in mass, related by E = Δmc². The neutrons released are included in the mass of the products.

questions.stem: A reactor operator slowly withdraws the control rods a little further while the reactor is running steadily. What happens?
options: Fewer neutrons are absorbed, so the fission rate and power output rise
More neutrons are absorbed, so the fission rate and power output fall
The neutrons are slowed more, so the fission rate stays exactly the same
The coolant flow increases, so the fission rate falls while the power rises
questions.explanation: With the rods further out, fewer neutrons are absorbed, so on average each fission causes slightly more than one more and the power rises. To hold the new power level the operator then adjusts the rods so the ratio returns to one.

questions.stem: Fission releases about 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J per uranium-235 nucleus, while burning releases about 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per carbon atom. About how many times more energy does one fission release than one carbon atom burning?
questions.explanation: 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹/(6.4 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 5.0 × 10⁷, so each fission releases about fifty million times as much energy as a chemical reaction involving one atom. Dividing the other way round gives 2.0 × 10⁻⁸.

questions.stem: Which is a genuine advantage of fission power stations over coal-fired stations?
options: They need no cooling water, so they can be built anywhere
They can be switched on and off instantly with no risk
They release almost no carbon dioxide while generating electricity
They produce no radioactive waste that needs long-term storage
questions.explanation: Fission produces no carbon dioxide during operation, which counts in its favour against fossil fuels. It does produce long-lived radioactive waste and needs large amounts of cooling water.

questions.stem: Which of these is a risk of using nuclear fission for power production?
options: Carbon dioxide emissions from burning the uranium fuel
Acid rain caused by sulfur dioxide released from the fuel
Explosions caused by the uranium fuel burning in oxygen
Accidental release of radioactive material if the core overheats
questions.explanation: If cooling fails, the core can overheat and radioactive material may escape, as happened at Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011. Uranium fuel is not burned, so it releases no carbon dioxide or sulfur dioxide.

questions.stem: Why does a reactor's coolant need to keep flowing for some time even after the chain reaction has been stopped?
options: The control rods release a burst of neutrons as soon as they are inserted
The moderator keeps on slowing neutrons, which releases more energy as heat
The steam left in the turbines flows back and heats the fuel rods
Radioactive fission products in the fuel keep decaying and releasing energy
questions.explanation: The fuel contains many radioactive fission products, and their decay keeps releasing energy, called decay heat, after fission stops. Without cooling this can melt the fuel, which is what happened at Fukushima when cooling was lost.

questions.stem: Why must spent nuclear fuel be stored safely for very long periods?
options: It contains a range of radioactive products, some with very long half-lives
It stays at a temperature of thousands of degrees for many millions of years
Its radioactivity increases over time until it is used again as fuel
It contains uranium-235 that can undergo spontaneous chain reactions
questions.explanation: Spent fuel contains many fission products and heavier elements such as plutonium. Some of these have half-lives of thousands of years or more, so the waste stays hazardous for a very long time. Its activity decreases, not increases, with time.

questions.stem: Which list gives requirements for the safe long-term storage of high-level nuclear waste?
options: Storage in thin plastic containers near the surface, for easy and cheap monitoring
Shielding, cooling, containment from groundwater and a geologically stable site
Burning in high-temperature furnaces to destroy the radioactive nuclei
Dilution in large volumes of seawater so the activity becomes negligible
questions.explanation: High-level waste emits penetrating radiation and decay heat, so it must be shielded and cooled. It must also be sealed so that radioactive material cannot leak into groundwater over thousands of years, ideally deep underground in stable rock. Heat and chemical processes cannot change half-life.

questions.stem: Why is high-level nuclear waste often first stored under several metres of water at the reactor site?
options: The water dissolves the waste so it can later be released
The water slows neutrons so a chain reaction can restart
The water cools the hot waste and absorbs its radiation
The water speeds up the decay so the waste becomes safe
questions.explanation: Freshly removed fuel is intensely radioactive and gives off decay heat. Water both removes the heat and acts as shielding. Nothing done to the waste changes its half-life.

questions.stem: A waste isotope has a half-life of about 30 years. About how long until its activity falls to about one-thousandth of its starting value?
options: About 30 000 years
About 60 years
About 3000 years
About 300 years
questions.explanation: After 10 half-lives the activity is (1/2)¹⁰ = 1/1024, about one-thousandth. Ten half-lives of 30 years is about 300 years. Waste with much longer half-lives stays hazardous for far longer.

questions.stem: Synroc, a material developed in Australia for nuclear waste, locks radioactive atoms into the crystals of a synthetic rock. Which requirement of safe storage does this mainly address?
options: Making the waste emit less heat in the first few years after use
Producing extra energy from the waste as it continues to decay
Preventing radioactive material leaching into groundwater over long periods
Shortening the half-lives of the radioactive isotopes in the waste
questions.explanation: Immobilising the waste in a durable, water-resistant solid makes it very hard for radioactive atoms to dissolve and travel with groundwater. No storage method changes half-lives.

questions.stem: The half-life of a radioactive isotope in nuclear waste depends on which of these?
options: The chemical compound it is in, so reprocessing can shorten it
The pressure in the storage site, so deep burial shortens it
Only the isotope itself; heat, pressure and chemical state do not change it
The temperature of the waste, so heating it shortens the half-life
questions.explanation: Half-life is a property of the nucleus and is independent of the physical and chemical state of the material. This is why waste cannot be made safe faster by heating, compressing or chemically treating it.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a nuclear fusion reaction?
options: An unstable nucleus emitting an alpha particle
Two heavy nuclei joining to form a very heavy nucleus
Two light nuclei joining to form a single heavier nucleus
A heavy nucleus splitting into two lighter nuclei
questions.explanation: In fusion, light nuclei such as isotopes of hydrogen combine into a heavier nucleus such as helium, releasing energy because the products have less mass. Splitting a heavy nucleus is fission.

questions.stem: Why are extremely high temperatures needed for nuclear fusion?
options: The high temperature turns all the neutrons into protons so that the nuclei can join
Fusion only occurs in a liquid, and hydrogen is liquid only when hot
The nuclei need enough kinetic energy to overcome their electrostatic repulsion
The heat breaks the strong nuclear force that holds the light nuclei apart
questions.explanation: Nuclei are positively charged and repel strongly. Only at temperatures of millions of degrees do they move fast enough to get close enough for the short-range strong nuclear force to pull them together.

questions.stem: Which is a major challenge in using fusion to generate electricity?
options: Finding enough fuel, because deuterium is one of the rarest substances on Earth
Disposing of the large volumes of long-lived fission products that fusion creates
Stopping the reaction, because fusion cannot be halted once it has started
Containing a plasma of over 100 million degrees long enough to release net energy
questions.explanation: No material can touch such a hot plasma, so it must be held by strong magnetic fields, and keeping it hot and dense long enough to release more energy than is put in is very difficult. Deuterium is plentiful in seawater, and fusion does not produce fission products.
